blocks.text: MLflow is an open source platform for tracking machine learning experiments, versioning models, and managing the transition from a trained model to a deployed one, filling the experiment tracking and model registry needs that come up repeatedly across the fine-tuning workflows covered throughout this course.

This topic covers what MLflow actually logs during a training run, how its model registry manages the lifecycle from staging to production, and how it compares to Weights and Biases, covered in the next topic, as another widely used option.
1. What MLflow Tracking Captures
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472763802-645477663.png

MLflow tracking records the details of a training run as it happens, connecting to the experiment tracking concept covered in an earlier topic, giving a structured, searchable record of what was tried and how it performed, rather than relying on scattered notes or memory.
2. Hyperparameters, Metrics, and Artifacts
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472763802-661342764.png

A single MLflow run logs the hyperparameters used, learning rate, batch size, LoRA rank covered in earlier modules, the metrics tracked during training, loss curves, evaluation scores covered throughout this course, and artifacts, saved model checkpoints, plots, or other output files, all tied together under one queryable run record.

code.content:
import mlflow

with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_param("learning_rate", 2e-5)
    mlflow.log_param("lora_rank", 16)
    mlflow.log_metric("eval_loss", 0.42)
    mlflow.log_artifact("./checkpoint")

blocks.text: 3. Comparing Runs Side by Side
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472764094-452099264.png

MLflow web interface lets several runs be compared directly, viewing how a specific hyperparameter change, a different learning rate for instance, affected the resulting metrics, turning what would otherwise be manual spreadsheet comparison into a built-in, structured workflow.
4. The MLflow Model Registry
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472764095-262839150.png

Beyond experiment tracking, MLflow includes a model registry that manages a model lifecycle through defined stages, staging for validation, production for the currently deployed version, and archived for retired versions, connecting to the model versioning concept covered in an earlier topic with a concrete tool implementation.

blocks.title: The registry gives version transitions an explicit, auditable record
blocks.content: Rather than informally deciding a new checkpoint is now the production model, moving a version through MLflow registry stages creates a clear, trackable history of what was deployed when.

blocks.text: 5. Self-Hosted vs Managed MLflow
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472764095-847384919.png

MLflow can be self-hosted, running the tracking server on infrastructure a team fully controls, or used through a managed service offered by several cloud providers, self-hosting offers more control and no vendor lock-in, a managed service reduces the operational burden of running the tracking infrastructure itself.
6. MLflow vs Weights and Biases
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472764095-903557836.png

MLflow and Weights and Biases, covered in the next topic, both solve the same core experiment tracking and model management problem, MLflow is open source and commonly self-hosted, Weights and Biases is primarily a hosted service with a strong collaborative visualization interface, the choice often comes down to whether a team prefers open source control or a more polished managed experience.
7. Serving a Model Directly From MLflow

blocks.alt: Serving a Model Directly From MLflow
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472764096-537147130.png

MLflow can spin up a local serving endpoint directly from a logged model artifact, useful for quick testing or lightweight deployment, though for the production-scale serving needs covered in the earlier Inference and Serving module, a dedicated framework like vLLM or TGI is generally the better production choice.
8. MLflow Across the Full Fine-Tuning Lifecycle

MLflow spans the full lifecycle covered across this course, tracking experiments during the training stages covered in earlier modules, managing which version is currently in production through its registry, connecting naturally to the monitoring and retraining pipeline concerns covered elsewhere in this module.
9. When MLflow Is a Good Fit

MLflow fits teams that want an open source, self-controllable experiment tracking and model registry solution, particularly teams already comfortable managing their own infrastructure who value avoiding vendor lock-in over the more polished managed experience some alternatives offer.
Worked Example

A team running many fine-tuning experiments with different LoRA ranks and learning rates logs each run to MLflow, capturing hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, and model checkpoints as artifacts, letting them compare all runs side by side in the MLflow interface rather than manually tracking results in a spreadsheet.

Once they identify their best performing run, they register that model in the MLflow registry, moving it through staging for validation and then to production, giving them a clear, auditable record of exactly which experiment produced their currently deployed model.
Common Mistakes

items: Not logging enough hyperparameters or metrics per run, making later comparison difficult or impossible
Using MLflow local model serving for significant production traffic instead of a dedicated serving framework
Skipping the model registry and informally tracking which checkpoint is in production, losing an auditable history
Choosing between MLflow and Weights and Biases without considering whether self-hosting control or a managed experience matters more to the team

blocks.text: Practice

For a fine-tuning experiment you are running or could imagine running, list the specific hyperparameters, metrics, and artifacts you would log to MLflow for each run, and describe how you would use the registry to manage the transition from your best experiment to a production deployment.
Key Takeaway

MLflow tracks fine-tuning experiments, logging hyperparameters, metrics, and artifacts per run for structured comparison, and manages the model lifecycle through a registry with staging, production, and archived stages, offering an open source, self-hostable alternative to the managed Weights and Biases experience covered in the next topic.
